articles.title: The Lawyer Who Picked A President, Then Switched Causes
articles.content:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day!

On Election Day, it’s worth recalling the case that settled a presidency in court rather than at the ballot box, Bush v. Gore (2000). Who was the lawyer who argued and won it for George W. Bush was a titan of the conservative legal movement, and he went on to serve as Bush’s solicitor general? Yet a few years later, he stunned his fellow conservatives by leading the legal fight to strike down California’s ban on same-sex marriage… alongside the very lawyer he had beaten in Bush v. Gore. 

Hint: His unlikely Proposition 8 partner was his old adversary in Bush v. Gore, David Boies.

See the answer on the next page.

The post The Lawyer Who Picked A President, Then Switched Causes appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: Your Client’s Best Evidence Might Be Sitting In Their Phone
articles.content:
I recently spoke at TASA about something I think personal injury lawyers should be paying much more attention to.
The client’s phone.
Not because we’re looking for some dramatic text message that wins the case. Usually, that’s not what we’re going to find.
What we may find is something better: a record of ordinary life.
Where someone went. Who they talked to. What they were doing. When they stopped doing it. Pictures they took without thinking about litigation. Work messages. Calendar entries. Notes. Receipts. Contacts. Sometimes years of little digital breadcrumbs that nobody created because they expected to need them as evidence someday.
That’s precisely what can make them valuable.
This is the third piece in a series I’ve been writing about the things that can shape a personal injury case long before anyone starts talking seriously about settlement or trial.
The first was about evidence that disappears.
The second was about why cases shouldn’t be treated as “settlement cases” from day one.
This one is about evidence that may already be sitting in your client’s hand.
Start With The Camera Roll
Ask someone what evidence is on their phone and they’ll probably think about text messages.
I usually think about photos.
Scroll through someone’s camera roll from the year before a serious injury and you can learn a surprising amount about that person’s life.
There might be pictures from vacations, children’s sporting events, nights out with friends, home projects, workouts, weekend trips or just ordinary Tuesday afternoons.
Then comes the injury.
Keep scrolling.
Sometimes you can actually see life getting smaller.
The trips stop. The golf pictures disappear. There aren’t as many photos from the kids’ games. The person who was always doing something is suddenly spending a lot more time at home.
Does that prove an injury?
Of course not.
But it may help tell a story that medical records alone can’t tell.
A medical chart can document a shoulder injury.
It can’t necessarily show you what that shoulder injury meant to the person who used to pick up his daughter, work on his house every Saturday or play softball twice a week.
The phone might.
What Were You Doing At 4:17?
Phones can also help with something much more basic: reconstructing a timeline.
Serious accidents are chaotic.
I’ve represented people who can remember certain moments with incredible clarity and have almost no memory of others. That’s not particularly surprising. They weren’t taking notes. They were living through an emergency.
Months later, lawyers start asking very specific questions.
When did you leave?
Who did you call?
Where have you been?
When did you first tell somebody you were hurt?
Did you take a picture?
Who else was there?
Now pick up the phone.
There may be a call at 4:17 p.m. A text at 4:22. A photo at 4:28. A map search. A rideshare receipt. A message to a spouse. A call to a supervisor saying you won’t make it to work.
Individually, these things can look trivial.
Put them together and sometimes you have a remarkably good timeline created by the person before anyone told them a timeline would matter.
That’s the kind of evidence I like.
The Witness You Forgot About
Here’s another common problem.
“Who was there?”
The client gives you three names.
Six months later, you’re looking through something on the client’s phone and another name appears.
“Oh, right. She was there too.”
People forget people.
Phones don’t always forget them.
A group text, contact, photo, call history or old message can help identify someone the client hadn’t thought about since the day of the incident.
That person may turn out to know nothing useful.
Or she may have seen exactly what happened.
You don’t know until you find her.
This is one reason I don’t think reviewing a client’s phone should mean hunting for one particular piece of evidence. Sometimes you’re trying to understand the ecosystem around the event.
Who was this person talking to?
Where were they?
What was happening in their life?
What changed afterward?
The answers may lead somewhere useful.
Work Lives On Phones Now Too
This has become especially important as the line between our phones and our workplaces has disappeared.
People text their bosses.
They get schedules through apps.
They receive work emails on their phones.
They communicate with customers. They photograph job sites. They keep calendars. Gig workers may have an enormous amount of their working history inside an app.
So when someone tells me an injury affected their ability to work, I don’t think only about tax returns and pay stubs.
Those documents matter.
But there may also be a much more immediate record.
A text saying, “I can’t take the shift tomorrow.”
A calendar that suddenly empties.
Messages asking coworkers to cover jobs.
Customers being rescheduled.
An independent contractor turning down work.
Again, none of these things necessarily proves the entire damages claim.
Evidence rarely works that neatly.
But it can corroborate what the client is telling you, and corroboration matters.
There’s Another Side To This
I can’t talk about phones and personal injury cases without mentioning the obvious problem.
The defense can be interested in them too.
Social media is the easiest example.
If someone claims she can barely walk and then posts a video of herself running a 10K, that’s going to be a problem.
But the issue is broader than telling clients, “Don’t post anything.”
I don’t like giving clients cute tricks for litigation. I want them to understand something much simpler.
Tell the truth.
Don’t exaggerate what you can’t do. Don’t minimize what you can do. Don’t try to manufacture a version of your life for a lawsuit.
And don’t start deleting things because you’re worried about how they might look.
If there’s something on the phone that concerns you, tell your lawyer.
I’d much rather learn about an uncomfortable photograph from my client than from opposing counsel at a deposition.
The phone isn’t automatically the plaintiff’s evidence.
It’s evidence.
Sometimes it helps. Sometimes it hurts. Usually, the lawyer needs to understand what’s there before deciding what matters.
Don’t Turn Your Client Into A Digital Crime Scene
There is a balance here.
A client’s phone may contain years of intensely private information that has absolutely nothing to do with the case.
The answer isn’t to vacuum up someone’s entire digital life because some portion of it could theoretically be useful.
You need a reason for what you’re looking for.
If the question is the client’s physical activity before and after an injury, look for evidence relevant to that.
If it’s lost income, focus on work.
If it’s the timeline surrounding a collision, reconstruct the timeline.
If you’re trying to identify witnesses, look for people connected to the event.
The goal isn’t more data.
It’s better evidence.
That’s an important distinction.
The Evidence We Create Without Knowing It
For most of human history, ordinary people didn’t keep detailed records of their ordinary days.
Now we do.
We just don’t call them records.
We call them texts.
Photos.
Calendars.
Apps.
Receipts.
Searches.
Messages.
Phones have quietly become diaries that we never intended to write.
For lawyers, that creates enormous responsibility. There are privacy issues. Discovery issues. Preservation issues. Context matters enormously. One isolated text or photograph can be misleading if you don’t understand what came before or after it.
But it also creates an opportunity to understand a client’s life in a way that wasn’t possible a generation ago.
Medical records can tell me what happened to someone’s body.
Employment records can tell me what happened to their paycheck.
A phone may help me understand what happened to their life.
And in a personal injury case, sometimes that’s the story we’re really trying to tell.
Amanda Demanda, Esq., is the founder of Amanda Demanda Injury Lawyers and a nationally recognized trial attorney with a focus on serious and catastrophic commercial truck accident litigation. She currently serves as President of the Miami-Dade Trial Lawyers Association. She has built one of the most visible plaintiff firms in the country, with offices in Miami, Tampa, Houston, Dallas, and throughout Florida and Texas, allowing her team to handle high-stakes cases across key transportation corridors. Known for blending courtroom skill with strategic insight, Amanda brings a people-first, safety-driven approach to complex trucking and personal injury cases, with a focus on accountability and real-world impact.

articles.title: No Soup For You! 5 ‘Seinfeld’ Lessons Every Lawyer Needs To Learn About Business Development
articles.content:
I’m a huge “Seinfeld” fan. I’ve probably seen every episode four or five times, and even today, certain scenes make me laugh as hard as they did when I first watched them. I even have a poster with “Seinfeld”-isms behind me in my office, which was a gift from an amazing client. With all the streaming services and thousands of shows available, there’s still something special about Jerry, George, Elaine, and Kramer.
What’s even more interesting is that after more than 20 years of coaching lawyers on business development, I’ve realized that some of the funniest moments from “Seinfeld” offer surprisingly useful lessons about growing a law practice.
Now, I realize that taking business advice from four dysfunctional New Yorkers might seem questionable but hear me out. Here are five classic “Seinfeld” moments that every lawyer looking to build a stronger book of business should consider.
1. Jerry’s Telemarketer: Stop Selling To People Who Don’t Want To Be Sold
The scene involves Jerry receiving an unwanted call from a telemarketer. Rather than simply hanging up, Jerry suggests calling the telemarketer at home later that evening. When the caller objects to being disturbed at home, Jerry makes his point and ends the conversation.
Brilliant! And surprisingly relevant to legal business development.
Nobody likes being sold to, especially when they haven’t expressed an interest or identified a need. Yet lawyers continue to approach prospective clients by talking about their firm’s accomplishments, listing their credentials, and explaining why they’re better than the competition.
My Sales-Free Selling methodology teaches lawyers to approach business development differently. Instead of pitching, convincing, and chasing, focus on building relationships, asking thoughtful questions, listening carefully, and understanding what prospective clients are trying to accomplish.
The same philosophy applies to marketing. Rather than constantly promoting yourself on LinkedIn, share helpful insights, demonstrate your expertise, and provide information that makes someone’s professional life easier.
When people see you as a trusted resource rather than another lawyer trying to sell something, you’ve already taken an important step toward earning their business.
2. The Contest: A Little Accountability Goes A Long Way
Who could forget the infamous episode where Jerry, George, Elaine, and Kramer enter a contest to see who can demonstrate the greatest self-control? I’ll leave the specifics out of this family-friendly article, but the competition itself is one of the funniest moments in television history.
The business development connection is simple. People tend to perform better when they have clear goals, accountability, and a little friendly competition.
I’ve seen this firsthand in my coaching groups, where attorneys share their business development objectives, discuss their progress, and challenge one another to improve. There’s something powerful about telling a group of peers that you’re going to accomplish something and then having to report back the following week.
Consider finding a fellow attorney or small group of professionals who want to grow their practices. Set measurable goals around networking meetings, strategic introductions, referral relationships, or new business opportunities. Then meet regularly to discuss what worked, what didn’t, and what needs improvement.
Business development can be a lonely undertaking, especially for solo practitioners. Having others involved creates structure, motivation, and the kind of accountability that turns good intentions into meaningful results. FYI, we also have a BE THAT LAWYER Community and Rainmaker Roundtables, which get ambitious lawyers out of their silos.
3. Yada, Yada, Yada: Your Business Development Plan Needs Details
Another classic “Seinfeld” moment occurs when George’s girlfriend skips over important parts of a story using the phrase “yada, yada, yada.” Unfortunately, the details she’s leaving out happen to be the most interesting and potentially incriminating parts of the conversation.
Lawyers do something similar when developing their business development plans.
They tell themselves they’re going to network more, get more referrals, improve their LinkedIn presence, and grow their book of business. Yada, yada, yada, they’ll have their best year ever.
The problem is that none of this constitutes an actual plan.
An effective legal business development plan should identify your ideal clients, the relationships you want to develop, the activities most likely to produce opportunities, and the time you’re willing to invest each week.
For example, instead of saying you’ll do more networking, identify five strategic referral partners you want to develop relationships with and schedule specific opportunities to connect. Rather than saying you’ll post more on LinkedIn, determine what content your ideal clients would find valuable and create a realistic publishing schedule.
You don’t need a 30-page business plan or an MBA to figure this out. A focused one- or two-page plan with specific actions, timelines, and measurable goals can make an enormous difference.
The details matter, and skipping them is often why lawyers struggle to produce consistent results.
4. Elaine’s Dancing: You Might Be Doing It Wrong And Not Know It
One of the most memorable episodes features Elaine dancing at an office party. She’s having the time of her life, completely unaware that everyone around her is horrified by her unusual moves.
While it’s hilarious to watch, there’s an important lesson here about self-awareness.
I’ve worked with plenty of lawyers who believe they’re excellent networkers or business developers, even though their approach may be turning people off.
Some dominate conversations, others hand out business cards like Halloween candy, and a few immediately start asking for referrals before establishing any meaningful relationship. What makes this particularly challenging is that many don’t recognize what they’re doing wrong.
The solution starts with getting honest feedback and becoming willing to improve.
Record yourself practicing a networking introduction, role-play a prospective client meeting, or ask a trusted colleague to evaluate your approach. Better yet, work with someone who understands professional services business development and can identify the habits holding you back.
The most successful rainmakers aren’t necessarily the most naturally gifted conversationalists. They’re often the lawyers willing to evaluate their performance, accept coaching, and continually sharpen their skills.
After all, nobody wants to be Elaine on the dance floor without realizing it.
5. The Soup Nazi: Know When To Walk Away
Lastly, who could forget the legendary Soup Nazi episode? The soup is apparently so delicious that customers are willing to tolerate the owner’s outrageous rules and behavior just to get a bowl.
When George fails to follow the process, he’s famously denied his soup.
While the scene is hysterical, it brings up an interesting question for lawyers. How much are you willing to tolerate to get what you want?
In legal business development, some attorneys spend years participating in networking groups they dislike, chasing prospective clients who never commit, or investing time in relationships that consistently fail to produce value.
They keep showing up because they believe something might eventually happen.
Sometimes the smartest business development decision is recognizing that a strategy, opportunity, or relationship isn’t working and making a change.
This doesn’t mean abandoning relationships because they haven’t immediately generated business. It means evaluating whether your time and energy are being invested in activities that align with your goals and have the potential to create meaningful results.
I’ve always encouraged lawyers to focus on building relationships with existing clients, trusted referral sources, and strategic partners who already know and appreciate their value. Often, the greatest opportunities are sitting right in front of you.
And if a particular networking group or prospect consistently leaves a bad taste in your mouth, perhaps it’s time to find another place to get your soup.
The Final Episode: Make Business Development Work for You
What I love most about “Seinfeld” is that its humor comes from everyday situations, awkward conversations, questionable decisions, and people who often lack the self-awareness to recognize their own mistakes.
Sound familiar?
The truth is that legal business development doesn’t have to be complicated, but it does require a willingness to approach things differently. When you stop selling and start building relationships, create accountability around your goals, develop a detailed plan, improve your interpersonal skills, and invest your time in the right opportunities, you dramatically improve your chances of building a successful practice.
So, whether you’re a Jerry, George, Elaine, or Kramer, there’s always room to become a better rainmaker.
And unlike the gang on Seinfeld, you don’t have to spend nine seasons making the same mistakes.
Build your book. Own your future. BE THAT LAWYER.
Steve Fretzin is a five-time bestselling author, host of the BE THAT LAWYER and Future Rainmakers podcasts, and a business development coach who works exclusively with attorneys. For more than 18 years, he has helped lawyers build strong books of business without selling, pitching, or chasing, using his proven Sales-Free Selling™ approach. His clients consistently become top rainmakers and credit his coaching and systems for driving meaningful, measurable growth. Steve can be reached directly at steve@fretzin.com, or through his website at bethatlawyer.com. Connect with him on LinkedIn at https://www.linkedin.com/in/stevefretzin. His ALL NEW BE THAT LAWYER Community is changing how lawyers develop the skills never taught in law school. Learn more at bethatlawyer.com/community.

For example, instead of saying you’ll do more networking, identify five strategic referral partners you want to develop relationships with and schedule specific opportunities to connect. Rather than saying you’ll post more on LinkedIn, determine what content your ideal clients would find valuable and create a realistic publishing schedule.

You don’t need a 30-page business plan or an MBA to figure this out. A focused one- or two-page plan with specific actions, timelines, and measurable goals can make an enormous difference.

The details matter, and skipping them is often why lawyers struggle to produce consistent results.

4. Elaine’s Dancing: You Might Be Doing It Wrong And Not Know It

One of the most memorable episodes features Elaine dancing at an office party. She’s having the time of her life, completely unaware that everyone around her is horrified by her unusual moves.

While it’s hilarious to watch, there’s an important lesson here about self-awareness.

I’ve worked with plenty of lawyers who believe they’re excellent networkers or business developers, even though their approach may be turning people off.

Some dominate conversations, others hand out business cards like Halloween candy, and a few immediately start asking for referrals before establishing any meaningful relationship. What makes this particularly challenging is that many don’t recognize what they’re doing wrong.

The solution starts with getting honest feedback and becoming willing to improve.

Record yourself practicing a networking introduction, role-play a prospective client meeting, or ask a trusted colleague to evaluate your approach. Better yet, work with someone who understands professional services business development and can identify the habits holding you back.

The most successful rainmakers aren’t necessarily the most naturally gifted conversationalists. They’re often the lawyers willing to evaluate their performance, accept coaching, and continually sharpen their skills.

After all, nobody wants to be Elaine on the dance floor without realizing it.

5. The Soup Nazi: Know When To Walk Away

Lastly, who could forget the legendary Soup Nazi episode? The soup is apparently so delicious that customers are willing to tolerate the owner’s outrageous rules and behavior just to get a bowl.

When George fails to follow the process, he’s famously denied his soup.

While the scene is hysterical, it brings up an interesting question for lawyers. How much are you willing to tolerate to get what you want?

In legal business development, some attorneys spend years participating in networking groups they dislike, chasing prospective clients who never commit, or investing time in relationships that consistently fail to produce value.

They keep showing up because they believe something might eventually happen.

Sometimes the smartest business development decision is recognizing that a strategy, opportunity, or relationship isn’t working and making a change.

This doesn’t mean abandoning relationships because they haven’t immediately generated business. It means evaluating whether your time and energy are being invested in activities that align with your goals and have the potential to create meaningful results.

I’ve always encouraged lawyers to focus on building relationships with existing clients, trusted referral sources, and strategic partners who already know and appreciate their value. Often, the greatest opportunities are sitting right in front of you.

And if a particular networking group or prospect consistently leaves a bad taste in your mouth, perhaps it’s time to find another place to get your soup.

The Final Episode: Make Business Development Work for You

What I love most about “Seinfeld” is that its humor comes from everyday situations, awkward conversations, questionable decisions, and people who often lack the self-awareness to recognize their own mistakes.

Sound familiar?

The truth is that legal business development doesn’t have to be complicated, but it does require a willingness to approach things differently. When you stop selling and start building relationships, create accountability around your goals, develop a detailed plan, improve your interpersonal skills, and invest your time in the right opportunities, you dramatically improve your chances of building a successful practice.

So, whether you’re a Jerry, George, Elaine, or Kramer, there’s always room to become a better rainmaker.

And unlike the gang on Seinfeld, you don’t have to spend nine seasons making the same mistakes.

Build your book. Own your future. BE THAT LAWYER.

Steve Fretzin is a five-time bestselling author, host of the BE THAT LAWYER and Future Rainmakers podcasts, and a business development coach who works exclusively with attorneys. For more than 18 years, he has helped lawyers build strong books of business without selling, pitching, or chasing, using his proven Sales-Free Selling™ approach. His clients consistently become top rainmakers and credit his coaching and systems for driving meaningful, measurable growth. articles.title: Till Dissolution Do Us Part: Inside Weil’s Biglaw Breakup
articles.content:
Ed. note: Welcome to our daily feature, Quote of the Day.
It’s the equivalent of managing hundreds of divorces because people get really emotional. A lot of these folks could never imagine what’s happening now.
— Al Togut, who served as lead counsel to Dewey & LeBoeuf in its bankruptcy, in comments given to Reuters about the emotional toll of dismantling a law firm. Weil plans an “orderly wind-down” outside bankruptcy, but sorting out partners’ financial obligations and entitlements can still take years. Breaking up is hard to do, especially when everyone involved is a lawyer.
